# Disney Selling $8 Million Super Bowl Ad Spots Despite Advertiser Pushback

[Shannen Ace](https://wdwnt.com/author/shannen-michaelsen/)

Published: June 3, 2026

![Image 3: ESPN logo on red pairs with the NFL shield on white, highlighting Disney’s connection to the Super Bowl.](https://r2-media.wdwnt.com/2025/08/ESPN-NFL-Agreement.png)

# Disney Selling $8 Million Super Bowl Ad Spots Despite Advertiser Pushback

Disney has sold some Super Bowl LXI commercial spots for about $8 million amid pushback from advertisers.

Disney first tried to set a [price of $10 million](https://variety.com/2026/tv/news/disney-10-million-super-bowl-commercials-advertisers-balk-1236723850/), then [$9 million](https://variety.com/2026/tv/news/super-bowl-soap-opera-disney-sells-commercials-9-million-1236747798/). Though they have sold some spots at these values, advertisers and marketers resisted. People familiar with recent negotiations told [Variety](https://variety.com/2026/tv/news/disney-super-bowl-commercials-8-million-advertising-1236765500/) that the company has now sold a “significant chunk” of 30-second spots for about $8 million each.

Disney and ESPN [reached a deal with the NFL](https://wdwnt.com/2025/08/disney-nfl-billion-dollar-deal-super-bowl/) last summer, and their first Super Bowl since 2026 will air on February 14, 2027 —the [culmination of a year of programming](https://wdwnt.com/2026/02/disney-espn-the-year-of-the-super-bowl-will-include-disney-parks-characters-storytelling-yearlong-programming/).

According to media buyers, the advertisers who bought $9 million units were largely “independents” new to the Super Bowl who don’t have long-term relationships with Disney.

Returning Super Bowl advertisers usually enjoy first pick of the next year’s spots. Disney reportedly didn’t want to offer this perk, leading to “a bit of disarray,” according to one media buyer.

Still, a source told Variety that Disney has sold 50% of their game-time inventory already.

“We have seen strong early demand from emerging categories driving double-digit units at $9 million each in addition to spending across Disney’s football portfolio,” Disney said in a statement. “Advertisers are leaning in early, recognizing the unmatched scale and cultural impact of the game with investment coming from seven major categories, led by A.I., finance, and pharma.”

Are you excited to watch the Super Bowl on ESPN? Let us know on social media.

# Advertisers Push Back on Disney Seeking $10 Million for 30-Second Super Bowl Commercial

An exclusive report from Variety indicates that advertisers are pushing back on Disney’s initial $10 million ask for a 30-second commercial slot for 2027’s Super Bowl LXI.

## Super Bowl LXI Commercials

[![Image 4: Super Bowl LXI logo surrounded by Disney, Pixar, Marvel, Star Wars, and Fox characters. The text says, "We're Going to the Super Bowl."](https://r2-media.wdwnt.com/2026/04/disney-were-going-to-the-super-bowl-campaign.jpg)](https://r2-media.wdwnt.com/2026/04/disney-were-going-to-the-super-bowl-campaign.jpg)
Super Bowl LXI, taking place in Los Angeles in 2027, will be hosted by [Disney’s ESPN for the first time in 20 years](https://wdwnt.com/2026/02/disney-espn-the-year-of-the-super-bowl-will-include-disney-parks-characters-storytelling-yearlong-programming/). Disney is planning on broadcasting the game on ABC and ESPN with a separate “alterna-cast” led by Peyton and Eli Manning on ESPN2. Super Bowl LXI will also be playing on Valentine’s Day (February 14), which Disney sees as a big opportunity to bring everyone together.

As such, Disney has started their initial ask for $10 million for a single 30-second commercial slot. Advertisers are pushing back against this amount, even though Super Bowl ad prices have steadily increased in the past few years. For reference, Super Bowl ads sold for around $5 million in 2016.

2026 Super Bowl LX top sales executive Mark Marshall revealed that NBC sold a handful of commercial slots for over $10 million. However, the initial starting price was $7 million, which sparked so much demand that there was too much interest in too little supply, driving the price higher and higher. The bulk of commercial slots were actually sold between $7 million and $8 million.

Disney remains optimistic and claims they are in active conversations and have “more requests than inventory to sell,” but registrations are not the same as orders. In recent years, broadcasters like NBC and Fox have managed to sell 40% to 60% of their ad schedule before the sale season kicks off in May, but Disney has not made similar progress so far. Another potential problem for Disney is that they lack a Super Bowl sales expert, someone who manages sales for the game.

What do you think of Disney’s initial commercial bid amount? Let us know on social media.

# Disney reportedly seeks $10 million for 30-second ads in Super Bowl LXI

> Advertisers are pushing back at the $10 million ask for a 30-second Super Bowl LXI spot.

![Image 5: The Disney+ logo and the Super Bowl LXI logo. Credit: USA Today Syndication; NFL](https://cdn1.thecomeback.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/94/2026/04/Disney-Super-Bowl-832x447.jpg)Credit: USA Today Syndication; NFL

Disney is aiming high with its asking price for 30-second ad spots in the 2027 telecast of Super Bowl LXI, which marks the company’s first time televising the Super Bowl in 20 years. Perhaps too high, according to potential buyers.

[_Brian Steinberg of Variety_ reports](https://variety.com/2026/tv/news/disney-10-million-super-bowl-commercials-advertisers-balk-1236723850/)that Disney “has told advertisers it believes they should pay $10 million for a 30-second ad in the company’s 2027 telecast of Super Bowl LXI, according to four people with knowledge of recent negotiations, but the high price tag has some marketers sitting on the sidelines.”

The game will also be simulcast on ABC, which last showed the Super Bowl in 2006. And there will be a _ManningCast_ of Super Bowl LXI, featuring Peyton and Eli Manning as commentators, on ESPN2.

Joe Buck, the ESPN play-by-play commentator for Super Bowl LXI, has referred to it as “[the biggest day in ESPN history](https://awfulannouncing.com/nfl/joe-buck-super-bowl-lxi-biggest-day-espn-history.html),” and[the network has gone all-out in promoting](https://awfulannouncing.com/espn/year-of-super-bowl-storytelling-initiatives-2027.html) the game [since the moment Super Bowl LX ended](https://awfulannouncing.com/espn/handoff-super-bowl-sofi-stadium-disneyland.html).

One of the people familiar with the Disney conversations told _Variety_ that “there is a big delta from where they started to where advertisers want to be,” regarding the $10 million initial ask.

According to Steinberg, _Variety_ also hears from sources that Disney “also sought a $10 million match of funds that would be spent elsewhere in its media portfolio,” which could involve “broader packages of its overall media portfolio, and a range of sports inventory that includes such things as MLB.TV and _Monday Night Football_.”

That all could lead to more complex and detailed discussions, which, to go with the reported balked-at asking price, could lead to a delay in reaching these deals. And that might make it difficult for Disney to sell a large amount of its ad inventory before its annual upfront presentation on May 12, 2026, whereas Fox and NBC were able to sell 40-60 percent of their Super Bowl inventory by then in recent years.

While Disney’s initial asking price is $10 million, [NBC’s initial ask was in the neighborhood of $7 million](https://awfulannouncing.com/nbc/bundle-super-bowl-olympics-ad-inventory.html) for a 30-second spot last March ahead of Super Bowl LX, which led to high demand from potential buyers. Steinberg reports that “the bulk of [NBC’s] Super Bowl ad inventory sold for $7 million to $8 million, according to people familiar with the matter,” though NBC claimed to sell a “handful” of spots for $10 million-plus. Last July, it was reported that [NBC was selling ad spots for $8 million](https://awfulannouncing.com/nfl/nbc-selling-super-bowl-ads-8-million.html) after selling out of units priced at $7 million ahead of the upfront season.

Steinberg adds that a common complaint among the four people familiar with conversations is that Disney “lacks a Super Bowl sales expert, someone who has managed sales for the Big Game for multiple years.”

So, it’s possible that Disney’s inexperience with hosting the Super Bowl telecast could further complicate things in this process.

In 2025, [Fox generated over $800 million in ad revenue](https://awfulannouncing.com/fox/800-million-super-bowl-advertising-revenue.html) after televising Super Bowl LIX. It will be fascinating to see if Disney can succeed in getting advertisers to meet the desired asking price, as well as where the ad revenue number ultimately lands.

results.title: Super Bowl Ad Cost in 2027
results.markdown:
Title: Super Bowl Ad Cost in 2027

URL Source: https://www.moonb.io/blog/super-bowl-commercial-cost

Published Time: 2026-10-11T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
A 30-second Super Bowl commercial cost about $8 million in airtime for the 2026 game on NBC, and a handful of spots went for $10 million or more, which had never happened before. For Super Bowl LXI on February 14, 2027, Disney asked $10 million per spot and most of them reportedly sold for $8 to $9 million. Making the ad and paying the people in it comes on top, and for a big-name spot the whole campaign can run from $15 million to $50 million.

I work at Moonb, a creative studio, and every January someone forwards me a Super Bowl ad with a note that says “can we do something like this?” Usually they mean the creative, and sometimes they mean the airtime too. So this guide answers both halves: what the network charges for the slot, what the ad itself costs to make, how the price got here, and the smaller ways into the game that cost a fraction of $8 million.

## A 30-second spot costs about $8 million

The national price for 30 seconds has sat around $8 million for two years running, after climbing roughly $1 million every couple of years before that. Networks never publish a rate card, so every number below comes from buyers and the trade press, and the top spots always sell above the average.

| Year | Game and network | Reported price for 30 seconds | Average audience |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2027 | LXI, ESPN and ABC | $8M to $9M for most spots, after Disney asked $10M | Not yet played |
| 2026 | LX, NBC | About $8M on average, a few at $10M or more | 125.6 million |
| 2025 | LIX, Fox | $8M for the top spots, a record at the time | 127.7 million |
| 2024 | LVIII, CBS | $6.5M to $7M, some above $7M | 123.7 million |
| 2023 | LVII, Fox | $6M to $7M, the peak above $7M | 115.1 million |
| 2022 | LVI, NBC | Some spots at $7M | 112.3 million |
| 2021 | LV, CBS | About $5.5M | 96.4 million |

The 2026 first, the $10 million spot, came from NBCUniversal’s own ad sales chief, who told [Adweek](https://www.adweek.com/convergent-tv/nbcuniversal-first-10-million-super-bowl-ads/) how a handful of buyers paid it. For 2025, Fox sold at least ten spots at $8 million each, [according to CNBC’s reporting via NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/business-news/super-bowl-ads-beckon-8-million-apiece-fox-rcna189801). The audience column comes from Nielsen, whose [2025 release](https://www.nielsen.com/news-center/2025/super-bowl-lix-makes-tv-history-with-over-127-million-viewers/) recorded the biggest average audience in TV history, 127.7 million people, and whose final count for [the 2026 game](https://www.nielsen.com/news-center/2026/nielsen-super-bowl-lx-final-viewership-rises-to-125-6-million-viewers-with-verified-big-data/) landed at 125.6 million.

One thing I always point out when a client reads a table like this: prices rise as the game gets closer. Networks sell the first spots in spring and summer and add to the price as inventory runs out, so two brands sitting next to each other in the same break can have paid very different amounts.

## Super Bowl LXI sold out in August 2026

Every 30-second slot in the 2027 game was gone by August 5, 2026, more than six months before kickoff. Disney sold the game across ESPN and ABC, the first time ESPN has carried a Super Bowl, and [its advertising arm announced](https://press.disneyadvertising.com/disney-advertising-concludes-2026-2027-upfront-and-sells-out-of-super-bowl-lxi-inventory) 58 brands across 34 categories, nine of them advertising in the game for the first time. The game itself is at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

That sell-out came about a month earlier than NBC managed for 2026 and around three months earlier than Fox for 2025, [Front Office Sports reported](https://frontofficesports.com/article/disney-sells-out-of-super-bowl-lxi-ad-inventory/), which also said Disney opened at $10 million per spot and settled at $8 million to $9 million for many of them after buyers pushed back. Disney itself has not published a price.

What that means in practice: if a brand wants national airtime in the big game, the decision gets made in the spring, nearly a year before the ad runs. The creative, in my experience, often gets finished in the last few months before the game, which is why some Super Bowl campaigns feel rushed even with that much money behind them.

Airtime is the number everyone quotes, but it is only the media bill. A big-game campaign also pays for the production, the talent, the music and everything that promotes the ad before and after the game. [CNN put the total](https://www.cnn.com/2024/02/09/media/what-celebrities-are-paid-for-super-bowl-ads) for a star-led Super Bowl commercial at $15 million to $50 million, with $10 million to $15 million of that going to the talent alone.

| What you pay for | Reported range | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 30 seconds of national airtime | About $8M (2026), $8M to $9M (2027) | Adweek, Front Office Sports |
| A cameo from a famous face | $25,000 to $10M | A talent agent at WME, via CNN |
| Most bigger stars | $1M to $3M | A talent agent at WME, via CNN |
| The top celebrity fees | About $10M | CNN |
| The whole campaign, star-led | $15M to $50M | CNN |

The talent figures come from Tim Curtis at the talent agency WME, who told CNN that cameos run from $25,000 to $10 million, that most bigger stars get $1 million to $3 million, and that the shoots usually take one or two days. CNN also reported that Ben Affleck was paid about $10 million for Dunkin’s 2023 spot.

On the production side, I can tell you where the money goes, because the line items are the same ones we see on any commercial, only bigger. The director and the crew, the cast and their usage rights, the set or location, visual effects, the music license, the edit and the color grade, and then all the versions: a 60-second cut, a 15-second cut, vertical and square versions for social, the teaser that runs a week before the game. On a big-game spot, that last group is where I see budgets grow the most, because the ad has to work on YouTube and social for weeks after the 30 seconds on TV. Our breakdown of [what a 30-second commercial costs](https://www.moonb.io/blog/how-much-is-a-30-second-commercial) walks through those lines for a normal broadcast spot, and the [video production cost guide](https://www.moonb.io/blog/video-production-cost) covers the rest of the range.

Measured per viewer, the price is lower than it sounds: about $64 for every thousand people watching in 2026, against roughly $58 in 2022. That is my own arithmetic, dividing the reported average price by Nielsen’s average audience, and since Nielsen changed how it measures in both 2025 and 2026, treat the trend as approximate.

| Year | Price for 30 seconds | Average audience | Cost per 1,000 viewers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2022 | $6.5M | 112.3 million | About $58 |
| 2023 | $7M | 115.1 million | About $61 |
| 2024 | $7M | 123.7 million | About $57 |
| 2025 | $8M | 127.7 million | About $63 |
| 2026 | $8M | 125.6 million | About $64 |

The reason brands keep paying is that nothing else on TV gathers that many people live, all at once, watching the ads on purpose. NBC News’s Jesse Kirsch looked at exactly that question in 2025, why companies spend record amounts on a TV event while viewers move to streaming, and the piece is worth four minutes:

Where I push back with clients is on the creative. The airtime buys the audience, and what the ad does with that audience decides whether the money comes back. The research we pulled together for [our 2026 Brand Creative Report](https://www.moonb.io/brand-creative-report/2026#s-3-5) points the same way: positive-emotion campaigns have been associated with 47% higher return on ad spend and six times the lift in intent to act. An $8 million slot with a forgettable ad is the most expensive way I know to waste a media budget, and the ads people still talk about in March are almost always the ones with one clear idea and a feeling attached to it. If you want examples, our list of [the best recent TV commercials](https://www.moonb.io/blog/best-tv-commercials) includes several big-game spots worth studying.

## Ways into the game for less than $8 million

You do not need a national spot to advertise during the Super Bowl. Local TV stations sell a small share of the breaks in their own markets, there are pregame and postgame slots, and since 2024 the streams have sold some ads of their own.

| Option | Reported price | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local spot in a smaller market | From about $10,000 to $50,000 | The game audience in one city |
| Local spot in a top market | Around $1.4M | New York, Chicago or San Francisco only |
| Pregame, just before kickoff | Up to $4.5M (2025) | A big live audience, before the game starts |
| Postgame | About $4M (2025) | The audience that stays on |

Title: TV Advertising Trends for Small Businesses (2026)

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/tv-advertising-trends-2026-smbs

Published Time: 2026-03-05T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
The predictions are over. We're well into 2026, and the trends that were once speculative are now producing real results for small businesses running TV ads. Instead of guessing what might happen, let's look at what's working, what's changed, and where the biggest opportunities are sitting right now.

This isn't a forecast. If you're looking for predictions, we've already covered that. This is a rundown of the trends that are driving measurable results for SMBs in 2026, backed by real data.

![Image 1: TV Advertising Trends 2026: What's Working for SMBs - Body1](https://media.adwave.com/fia320z3blxi/2IQcTR6OiZuhxASrC1crxe/e86b51689cbf99b5408338c95a19f54b/body1.png)
[Connected TV advertising](https://adwave.com/resources/what-is-connected-tv-advertising) has been growing for years, but 2026 is the year SMBs went from curious to committed. U.S. CTV ad spending is projected to reach $33.35 billion in 2026, up from $28.75 billion in 2025 (Statista, 2025). That's a 16% jump year over year.

What's different now is who's spending. It's not just enterprise brands anymore. According to the IAB's 2025 Video Ad Spend & Strategy Report, 55% of digital video buyers planned to increase their CTV budgets in 2025, with small and mid-size advertisers representing the fastest-growing buyer segment. That momentum has carried directly into 2026.

The barrier to entry has dropped dramatically. Platforms like Adwave let you launch a TV campaign with as little as $50, which means a local plumber or neighborhood bakery can run on the same premium networks as national brands. A few years ago, that would've sounded unrealistic. Now it's just Tuesday.

The single biggest unlock for small businesses in TV advertising? AI-generated creative. Creating a broadcast-quality commercial used to cost $5,000 to $50,000 or more. Now you can generate a polished 30-second spot in about two minutes.

This isn't a gimmick. According to Magna Global's 2025 advertising forecast, AI-generated creative tools contributed to a measurable increase in first-time TV advertisers entering the market. Small businesses that never considered TV are now running ads because the creative bottleneck simply doesn't exist anymore.

With Adwave, you drop in your website URL (or your Yelp page, or a social media profile), and the platform builds a professional ad from your existing content. No agency. No film crew. No six-week production timeline. The quality is strong enough to run across 100+ premium channels, and the speed means you can test messaging quickly instead of betting everything on one concept.

## Self-Serve Platforms Have Replaced the Old Gatekeepers

![Image 2: TV Advertising Trends 2026: What's Working for SMBs - Body2](https://media.adwave.com/fia320z3blxi/7miTDOmy9i9KBx4tQiHkvI/25fe85c6a464eb62d2459b6e694da29d/body2.png)
TV advertising used to require phone calls to sales reps, long contracts, and minimum spends that started in the thousands. In 2026, self-serve [CTV advertising platforms](https://adwave.com/resources/ctv-advertising-platforms) have made that model feel like a relic.

The shift to self-serve isn't just about convenience. It's about control. You set your own budget, pick your targeting, launch when you're ready, and see performance data in real time. No middleman markup. No waiting for a quarterly report to find out if your campaign worked.

According to eMarketer, programmatic CTV (which includes self-serve platforms) now accounts for more than 75% of all CTV ad transactions in the U.S. (eMarketer, 2025). That's up from roughly 60% just two years ago. The buying model has fundamentally shifted, and small businesses are the ones benefiting most.

## Local Targeting Is Getting Sharper

One of the biggest knocks against TV advertising for small businesses used to be waste. Why pay to reach an entire metro area when you only serve a 15-mile radius? That argument doesn't hold up anymore.

CTV platforms now offer ZIP code-level and even household-level targeting. You can reach viewers in specific neighborhoods, filter by interests and demographics, and layer in first-party data to build highly specific audiences. According to Nielsen's 2025 State of Play report, 68% of CTV ad impressions are now delivered with some form of advanced audience targeting beyond basic age and gender.

For a local business, this changes the math completely. You're not paying for eyeballs you don't need. You're reaching the people who are most likely to walk through your door, and you can measure whether they do.

## Measurement Has Caught Up with the Medium

![Image 3: TV Advertising Trends 2026: What's Working for SMBs - Body3](https://media.adwave.com/fia320z3blxi/23NjDwP3y5Zi2BMAgtkXY3/b951b906c5fd7550ffaab08a0ee23ef0/body3.png)
For years, the biggest criticism of TV advertising was that you couldn't track it the way you could a Google or Meta ad. That gap has closed significantly in 2026.

Attribution tools now connect TV ad exposure to website visits, app downloads, store visits, and even online purchases. According to the IAB's 2025 Measurement & Attribution Report, 72% of CTV advertisers now use multi-touch attribution models, up from 48% in 2023. Platforms are reporting on incremental reach, view-through conversions, and cross-device engagement.

For SMBs, this means you don't have to take TV advertising on faith. You can see what's working, what isn't, and adjust accordingly. If you want to dig deeper into how measurement works, check out our guide on [CTV advertising growth and where it's heading](https://adwave.com/resources/ctv-advertising-growth-rate).

## FAST Channels Are Creating New Inventory (and Lower Prices)

Free ad-supported streaming TV (FAST) channels have exploded. Platforms like Tubi, Pluto TV, and the Roku Channel now collectively reach over 100 million monthly viewers in the U.S. (Variety, 2025). That's a massive pool of ad-supported inventory that simply didn't exist at this scale three years ago.

Why does this matter for small businesses? More inventory means more affordable pricing. The average [CPM across streaming platforms](https://adwave.com/resources/tv-advertising-cpm-by-platform) ranges from $15 to $35, but FAST channels tend to sit on the lower end of that range. You're getting premium-feeling placements at rates that rival digital display advertising.

FAST viewership continues to climb as consumers look for ways to cut subscription costs. According to Parks Associates, 62% of U.S. broadband households used at least one FAST service in 2025, up from 50% the prior year. For advertisers, this growing audience represents a chance to reach engaged viewers who are actively choosing to watch content, not just scrolling past it.

## Interactive and Shoppable TV Ads Are Gaining Traction

TV ads used to be a one-way conversation. You watched, and maybe you remembered the brand later. In 2026, interactive ad formats are changing that dynamic.

QR codes on TV ads have become standard practice. According to a 2025 study by LG Ad Solutions, QR code scan rates on CTV ads increased 42% year over year, with the highest engagement coming from local service and retail advertisers. Viewers are now conditioned to scan, and advertisers are building campaigns around that behavior.

Beyond QR codes, shoppable overlays and click-to-action formats are rolling out across major [streaming TV advertising platforms](https://adwave.com/resources/best-streaming-tv-advertising-platforms). These formats let viewers engage with an ad directly through their remote or connected device, whether that's requesting a quote, browsing a menu, or adding a product to their cart.

For small businesses, interactive formats bridge the gap between awareness and action. Your TV ad doesn't just build brand recognition. It can drive a measurable response in the moment.

The 2024 election cycle dumped an estimated $12.3 billion into political advertising, with CTV absorbing a record share (AdImpact, 2025). That surge tightened inventory, drove up CPMs, and pushed some SMB advertisers to the sidelines during Q3 and Q4 of 2024.

Political spending has largely cleared from the system. CPMs have normalized, inventory is wide open, and the first half of 2026 is one of the most favorable buying windows for small businesses in recent memory. If you paused your TV advertising during election season, now's the time to get back in.

The other lasting effect: political campaigns proved that CTV works for hyper-local targeting at scale. The same ZIP code targeting and audience segmentation that campaigns used to reach swing voters is now available to any small business looking to reach its own neighborhood.
